extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students and instructors in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, constructions, and computational consequences for the universal coefficient theorem and the Künneth formula in homology: properties of Tor, cross product constructions, sign/orientation conventions, and exact/semi-exact sequences used to compute homology of products and with coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3A.4: Universal coefficient split exact sequence (homology)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each pair of spaces (X,A) there are split exact sequences 0 → H_n(X,A) ⊗ G → H_n(X,A; G) → Tor(H_{n-1}(X,A), G) → 0 for all n, natural with respect to maps (X,A) → (Y,B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequence splits (so H_n(X,A;G) ≅ H_n(X,A)⊗G ⊕ Tor(H_{n-1}(X,A),G)), but the splitting is not natural; counterexamples show natural splitting cannot be expected in general (e.g., quotient map M(Z_m,n)→S^{n+1} with G=Z_m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (1): Symmetry of Tor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor(A,B) ≈ Tor(B,A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by applying the six-term exact sequence (item (6)) to a free resolution of one factor and using vanishing of Tor with free modules plus the five-lemma; uses natural commutativity of tensor product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (2): Tor commutes with direct sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor(⊕_i A_i, B) ≈ ⊕_i Tor(A_i, B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may choose the free resolution of ⊕_i A_i as the direct sum of free resolutions of the A_i's; direct-sum behavior of tensor and Tor follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (3): Vanishing of Tor for free or torsionfree factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor(A,B) = 0 if A or B is free, or more generally torsionfree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A is free there is a free resolution with higher terms 0, so Tor(A,B)=0. If B is free, tensoring a free resolution of A with B preserves exactness. The torsionfree generalization is proved by reduction to finitely generated torsionfree subgroups which are free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (4): Tor depends only on torsion subgroup of first factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor(A,B) ≈ Tor(T(A), B) where T(A) is the torsion subgroup of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the six-term exact sequence (item (6)) to 0 → T(A) → A → A/T(A) → 0 and use that A/T(A) is torsionfree (hence Tor with it vanishes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (5): Tor with Z_n
rubrics_metrics.description: Tor(Z_n, A) ≈ Ker(A --n--> A) (i.e., the n-torsion in A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comes from tensoring the free resolution 0 → Z --n--> Z → Z_n → 0 with A; in particular for finitely generated groups Tor(Z_m, Z_n) ≈ Z_gcd(m,n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. 3A.5 (6): Six-term exact sequence for Tor and tensor
rubrics_metrics.description: For each short exact sequence 0 → B → C → D → 0 there is a naturally associated exact sequence 0 → Tor(A,B) → Tor(A,C) → Tor(A,D) → A ⊗ B → A ⊗ C → A ⊗ D → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by tensoring a free resolution 0 → F_1 → F_0 → A → 0 with the short exact sequence and passing to the long exact homology sequence of chain complexes; naturality follows from functoriality of tensor and Tor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3A.6 (a): Homology with Q coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: H_n(X; Q) ≈ H_n(X; Z) ⊗ Q; when H_n(X; Z) is finitely generated, dim_Q H_n(X; Q) equals rank H_n(X; Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of universal coefficient theorem by tensoring with Q (Tor terms vanish with Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3A.6 (b): Homology with Z_p coefficients decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If H_n(X; Z) and H_{n-1}(X; Z) are finitely generated, then H_n(X; Z_p) has: (i) a Z_p summand for each Z summand of H_n(X; Z), (ii) a Z_p summand for each Z_{p^k} summand in H_n(X; Z), k ≥ 1, (iii) a Z_p summand for each Z_{p^k} summand in H_{n-1}(X; Z), k ≥ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how free and torsion summands in integer homology contribute to homology over Z_p via tensor and Tor computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3A.7: Vanishing and coefficient detection
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) H_*(X; Z)=0 for all * iff H_*(X; Q)=0 and H_*(X; Z_p)=0 for all primes p. (b) A map f: X→Y induces isomorphisms on homology with Z coefficients iff it induces isomorphisms on homology with Q and with Z_p for all primes p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mapping cone and universal coefficient sequences; reduction to showing an abelian group A with A⊗Q=0 and Tor(A,Z_p)=0 for all p must be 0 by considering exact sequences for Z→Q and Z→Z_p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization to modules over a ring R: behavior of Tor
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing abelian groups by R-modules yields functors Tor^R_n(A,B); unlike R = Z, Tor^R_n(A,B) need not vanish for n>1 in general. If R is a PID, submodules of free modules are free and the algebra (including universal coefficient theorem and Künneth) goes through as over Z. If R is a field F, every module is free and Tor^F_n = 0 for n>0, so H_n(C ⊗_F G) ≈ H_n(C) ⊗_F G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the ring-dependence: PIDs behave similarly to Z; fields simplify because Tor vanishes beyond degree 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross product in homology (cellular definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For CW complexes X and Y, the cellular cross product gives a bilinear map Hi(X; R) × H_j(Y; R) → H_{i+j}(X × Y; R), defined by taking products of cellular chains and showing cycles map to cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined using cellular chains and the boundary relation d(a × b) = d a × b + (−1)^i a × d b; independence of cell structures follows from naturality and cellular approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary formula for products of cells
rubrics_metrics.description: For cellular chains, d(e_i × e_j) = d e_i × e_j + (−1)^i e_i × d e_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by checking the cube I^n case (explicit sign formula) and using naturality of cellular maps to reduce the general case to that special case; sign originates from orientation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation convention for product cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Orient the product I_i × I_j = I_{i+j} by choosing an ordered basis for I_i followed by an ordered basis for I_j; reversing orientation of either factor reverses orientation of the product—thus the order of factors matters and yields sign rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice leads to the (−1)^i sign in the boundary formula and to the graded-commutativity sign in cross products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3B.2 (Naturality of cross product under cellular maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cellular maps f: X→Z and g: Y→W, the induced chain maps satisfy (f × g)_* = f_* × g_*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces coefficient computations to degrees of maps S^i→S^i and uses deg(f ∧ g) = deg(f) deg(g) via suspension and smash-product arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic sign and graded-commutativity of cross product
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition of factors introduces a sign: if T: X×Y → Y×X is the swap, then T_*(a×b) = (−1)^{ij} b×a for a ∈ H_i(X), b ∈ H_j(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sign arises by moving i coordinates past j coordinates (ij transpositions), each contributing −1; cross product is bilinear and associative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3B.5: Algebraic Künneth formula for chain complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a PID and the R-modules C_i are free, then for each n there is a natural short exact sequence 0 → ⊕_i H_i(C) ⊗_R H_{n-i}(C') → H_n(C ⊗_R C') → ⊕_i Tor^R(H_i(C), H_{n-i-1}(C')) → 0, and this sequence splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: handle special case when boundaries in C are zero, then decompose C into Z and B subcomplexes (with trivial boundaries), use long exact sequence from short exact sequence 0→Z→C→B→0, identify kernels/cokernels with Tor and tensor pieces via free resolutions; splitting obtained assuming freeness (construct map to H(C)⊗H(C')). Naturality holds; splitting not necessarily natural in topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3B.6: Topological Künneth formula (CW complexes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are CW complexes and R is a PID, then there are natural split short exact sequences 0 → ⊕_i H_i(X;R) ⊗_R H_{n-i}(Y;R) → H_n(X × Y;R) → ⊕_i Tor^R(H_i(X;R), H_{n-i-1}(Y;R)) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows by applying the algebraic Künneth theorem to cellular chain complexes C_*(X) and C_*(Y) and using Proposition 3B.1 that C_*(X×Y) ≈ C_*(X) ⊗ C_*(Y). Splitting exists but is not natural in general; naturality of the sequence in the sense of maps between pairs holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3B.7: Künneth over a field
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a field and X,Y are CW complexes, then the cross product map ⊕_i H_i(X;F) ⊗_F H_{n-i}(Y;F) → H_n(X × Y;F) is an isomorphism for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over a field Tor terms vanish, so the short exact sequence reduces to an isomorphism; this simplifies computations considerably (e.g., for Q or Z_p coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Künneth formula (pairs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For CW pairs (X,A) and (Y,B) and R a PID there is a split short exact sequence 0 → ⊕_i H_i(X,A;R) ⊗_R H_{n-i}(Y,B;R) → H_n(X×Y, A×Y ∪ X×B;R) → ⊕_i Tor^R(H_i(X,A;R), H_{n-i-1}(Y,B;R)) → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the algebraic Künneth formula using the identification of relative cellular chain complexes: C_*(X×Y)/C_*(A×Y ∪ X×B) ≈ C_*(X)/C_*(A) ⊗ C_*(Y)/C_*(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced (smash product) Künneth formula and suspension case
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a reduced Künneth short exact sequence for smash products: 0 → ⊕_i i H_i(X;R) ⊗_R _{n-i}(Y;R) → _n(X ∧ Y; R) → ⊕_i Tor^R(_i(X;R), _{n-i-1}(Y;R)) → 0, and in particular H_{n+k}(X ∧ S^k; R) ≈ H_n(X;R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case when A,B are basepoints: identifies smash product homology with reduced tensor/Tor pieces; useful for Moore spaces and for defining homology with arbitrary coefficients via suspensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example 3B.4: Necessity of Tor term (torsion interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y have torsion in H_1 of orders m and n respectively (e.g., S^1 with a 2-cell attached by degree m), then H_2(X×Y) ≈ Z_q and H_3(X×Y) ≈ Z_q where q = gcd(m,n), and these homology groups correspond to Tor(H_1(X), H_1(Y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows cross product map Hi⊗H_{n-i} need not be surjective when both factors have torsion; the Tor summand accounts for the 'extra' homology classes not expressible as cross products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial cross product construction (singular chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chain-level cross product Cm(X;R) ⊗ Cn(Y;R) → C_{m+n}(X×Y;R) is constructed by subdividing the product simplex Δ^m × Δ^n into (m+n)-simplices indexed by monotone lattice paths σ and summing (−1)^{|σ|} (f × g) ∘ ℓ_σ over σ, giving ∂(f×g) = ∂f × g + (−1)^m f × ∂g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit combinatorial formula for the cross product in singular homology; the subdivision into simplices corresponds to paths in an m×n grid and the signs |σ| count squares under the path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology cross product via cellular cochains
rubrics_metrics.description: Define (φ × ψ)(e^k_α × e^ℓ_β) = φ(e^k_α) ψ(e^ℓ_β) and zero on other cells to obtain a cohomology cross product H^k(X;R) × H^ℓ(Y;R) → H^{k+ℓ}(X×Y;R); cup product can be defined from this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cellular cochain-level product is straightforward when using product cellular structures; relates to the cup product and dualizes the homology cross product constructions.
